description: Does the opt-in-only AGGRESSIVE bucket (Chain-of-Draft style, ~5-word reasoning steps) still correctly explain BOTH halves of a genuinely simple, single-fact code question, or does the pressure to be terse cause it to drop one side of the distinction? Deliberately the narrow, low-risk case brevity_injector.py's docstring says AGGRESSIVE has never been validated for -- this is that validation. Needs stage_config.brevity_injector.aggressive_for_task_types=['code'] (opt-in only, added 2026-09-06; without it AGGRESSIVE never fires at all). Prompt includes a real code fence (same fix as quality_adaptive_budget_002's history) so task_classifier actually lands this in 'code', not 'conversational' -- a prose-only version of this question has no code fence/keyword/traceback marker and gets classified conversational instead, silently never engaging the mechanism under test. required_elements broadened 2026-09-06 after a real run: the real (fully correct) response said 'compares values' rather than 'equal'/'equality'/'same value' -- a benchmark-harness gap, not a quality regression, but a real pattern worth naming: AGGRESSIVE's terse style favors compact phrasing a rubric written for normal-verbosity answers doesn't anticipate.

messages.content:
Given this Python code:
```python
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b, a is b)
```
What's the difference between `==` and `is` here?

judge_rubric: Rate 1-5 how correctly and completely the response distinguishes value-equality (==) from object-identity (is) under aggressive brevity pressure. A 5 correctly and clearly distinguishes both concepts even tersely; a 1 conflates them, gets the distinction backwards, or omits one side entirely.

description: Second AGGRESSIVE sample (2026-09-06), a different simple code gotcha -- broadening from n=1 before trusting the real +400-output-token result from quality_brevity_aggressive_001's scenario beyond one case. Same opt-in stage_config and code-fence requirement as _001.

messages.content:

description: Third AGGRESSIVE sample (2026-09-06), a two-sided distinction (like _001) but a different concept -- shallow vs. deep copy. Tests whether AGGRESSIVE drops one side of a two-part answer under terseness pressure, the same failure mode _001 was built to catch, on new content. required_elements broadened 2026-09-06 (third real instance of this same pattern, after _001 and _004): the real response correctly said 'shares inner lists with a; c fully independent' -- present-tense 'shares inner', not 'shared inner'/'share the inner'. Broadened generously this time (not just adding the one observed phrase) since exact-substring grading against AGGRESSIVE's terse, grammatically-compressed output has now shown this exact failure mode three times.

messages.content:
Given this Python code:
```python
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = a.copy()
c = copy.deepcopy(a)
```
What's the difference between `b` and `c`?

judge_rubric: Rate 1-5 how correctly and completely the response distinguishes the shallow copy `b` (shares the nested inner lists with `a`) from the deep copy `c` (fully independent nested lists) under aggressive brevity pressure. A 5 correctly distinguishes both sides even tersely; a 1 conflates them or omits one side entirely.

description: First HARD-end AGGRESSIVE sample (2026-09-06), per the user asking to test the broader 'code' category rather than just simple single-fact questions. A real bug-fix task with a genuine edge case (same shape as quality_adaptive_budget_001) -- does terseness pressure cause AGGRESSIVE to miss the edge case entirely or propose an incomplete/broken fix, the exact risk brevity_injector.py's docstring warns 'code' spans ('everything from a one-line fix to a multi-file design question')? required_elements broadened 2026-09-06 after a real run: the real response correctly diagnosed the bug AND gave a working fix (`if len(unique) < 2: return None`), but wrote '<2 unique values' (symbolic) rather than 'fewer than 2' (worded) -- a benchmark-harness gap, not a quality regression; AGGRESSIVE's terse style favors compact/symbolic notation a worded-phrase rubric didn't anticipate.

messages.content:
This function is supposed to return the second-largest unique value in a list, but it's buggy:
```python
def second_largest(nums):
    unique = list(set(nums))
    unique.sort()
    return unique[-2]
```
What's wrong with it and how do you fix it?

judge_rubric: Rate 1-5 how correctly and completely the response identifies the edge-case bug (fails when there are fewer than 2 unique values, raising IndexError) and provides a working fix, under aggressive brevity pressure. A 5 correctly diagnoses the edge case and fixes it even tersely; a 1 misses the edge case entirely or proposes a broken fix.

description: Second HARD-end AGGRESSIVE sample -- a genuine multi-point complexity/design explanation (WHY it's slow, i.e. exponential recomputation, PLUS a concrete fix, i.e. memoization/iteration), closer to the harder end of what 'code' can mean than any of the single-fact samples. Tests whether AGGRESSIVE's ~5-word-reasoning-step pressure causes it to drop either the diagnosis or the fix, not just state one of the two.
judge_rubric: Rate 1-5 how correctly and completely the response identifies WHY the recursive fib is slow (exponential time from repeated recomputation of the same subproblems) AND proposes a concrete way to fix it (memoization, iterative/DP, etc.), under aggressive brevity pressure. A 5 hits both the diagnosis and a real fix even tersely; a 1 misses either half.

description: Extending AGGRESSIVE validation to a new task type (2026-09-06), per the user asking to test + opt-in more task types rather than default it on for all of 'code'. Simple single-fact conversational question -- 'why is the sky blue' has one clear scientific answer (Rayleigh scattering). No code fence needed here (unlike the 'code' samples): task_classifier's conversational bucket is the weak, catch-all default (0.4 confidence, no special markers needed) so this classifies correctly with a plain question. required_elements broadened proactively (not reactively, having now seen this pattern three times on the code samples) to include the compact phrasing AGGRESSIVE tends to produce.
judge_rubric: Rate 1-5 how correctly the response explains why the sky is blue (shorter-wavelength blue light is scattered more by the atmosphere -- Rayleigh scattering) under aggressive brevity pressure. A 5 correctly identifies the scattering mechanism even tersely; a 1 gives a wrong or unrelated explanation.

description: Harder conversational AGGRESSIVE sample -- a genuine two-sided distinction (weather = short-term, climate = long-term average), same failure mode as the code copy/equality samples (does terseness drop one side of a two-part answer?), on a new task type and new content shape (no code at all). required_elements broadened 2026-09-06 after a real run: this time the WITHOUT-brevity_injector baseline failed, not an AGGRESSIVE response -- the real reply said 'day to day' (spaces) where the rubric expected 'day-to-day' (hyphenated). Correction to the earlier working theory: this exact-substring-grading fragility isn't an AGGRESSIVE-specific artifact, it can trip on any real response regardless of verbosity.
